reason: Attacked hard, because this was the weakest verdict of the four: the verifier says plainly that the novel was never opened and rests the wording on 'a sourced Wikiquote entry', and the brief's own rule 2 calls a standard reference 'a fame signal, never a verification'. Wikiquote is not an edition. So I went looking for print. The Left Hand of Darkness is still in copyright and there is no scan of it on the Internet Archive (an advanced search for the title and the author returns nothing, and every item whose title matches is audio or criticism), so I could not open the novel either. What I could do, and did, was search the full text of scanned printed books for the phrase 'taught as a child on my homeworld'. It occurs in 48 scanned volumes, and I read the surrounding text of twenty of them. The wording is confirmed letter for letter in independently typeset scholarly books that quote the novel directly, among them Understanding Ursula K. Le Guin (twice, pp. 234 and 278), Approaches to the Fiction of Ursula K. Le Guin (in two separate printings, pp. 190 and 194), Ursula K. Le Guin, Voyager to Inner Lands and to Outer Space (p. 238), Politics, Persuasion, and Pragmatism (p. 266), Future Females (p. 208), Science Fiction: Its Criticism and Teaching (p. 202) and 80!: Memories and Reflections on Ursula K. Le Guin (p. 244). All read 'I'll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination', with Truth capitalised and homeworld one word. Two outliers are OCR or house-styling noise and not a rival reading: one volume shows 'a matter of imagination' on a page that also shows 'a matter of the imagination', and one lowercases truth. That is a dozen independent printed witnesses in place of one wiki, so the wording stands and this line no longer rests on a fame signal. Attribution and speaker: undisputed, and the report is Genly Ai's, so naming him after the locator is right and there is no reporter-versus-speaker trap; Le Guin is on no line of the misattribution list. Scope: a novel first published 1969, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory, nothing needing a content warning, and at six in the morning it is a good opening for a month about saying what is there. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], person 'ursula k. le guin' yearCount 0, not banned, not at cap, no second Le Guin in the month's proposals or the June carry-ins. Mechanics: the source leads with the name, has no dash, no straight double quote, and runs 84 characters; the quotation ends in a full stop, uses a curly apostrophe in I'll, and is prose left unbroken; tag Fiction is the form of the work. The one real defect, which I record but do not think fatal: 'opening sentence' is loose. A full-text search for 'Transcript of Ansible Document' turns up five printed books that reproduce the head of the chapter, and they agree that chapter 1, A Parade in Erhenrang, BEGINS with an archival label, 'From the Archives of Hain. Transcript of Ansible Document 01-01101-934-2-Gethen: To the Stabile on Ollul: Report from Genly Ai, First Mobile on Gethen/Winter, Hainish Cycle 93, Ekumenical Year 1490-97', and only then comes the quoted line. One of those books, Politics, Persuasion, and Pragmatism, p. 266, says in so many words that the novel 'begins: From the Archives of Hain'. The label is a document heading and not a sentence, and every reference in print treats the quoted line as the novel's opening line, so the card is not making a false claim; but it is exactly precise to call it the first sentence of the report, which also justifies the speaker in parentheses. I give that in betterCitation as a refinement, not as a correction: nothing about the author, work, chapter or wording changes. Separately, the chapter title is Erhenrang, as the verifier wrote it, not Ehrenrang as Wikiquote has it; another reason not to let that page carry the verification.
betterCitation: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, chapter 1, first sentence of the report (Genly Ai)
